posts:
Almost nothing that got breached this year was breached by defeating cryptography.

Nobody factored a key. Nobody broke a cipher.

The maths held. The way we prove who we are did not.

Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, covering Nov 2024 to Oct 2025:

31% of breaches now START with a software vulnerability — which Verizon says has overtaken stolen passwords as the top way in.

That cuts against the lazy version of this argument, so say it plainly: "passwords are the whole problem" is no longer true at the point of entry.

Credentials are still enormous — ~39% of breaches involve credential abuse somewhere. But the front door changed.

Here's what's absent from every one of those lists: a row for "defeated the encryption."

It effectively doesn't happen.

The cryptography is the one component performing to spec. Everything failing around it is authentication, patching and human judgement.
We spend our anxiety on the one part of the stack that's working, and our budget on the parts that aren't.

Now the structural problem with the login model most of the internet runs on.

Whatever you use to sign in, there's almost always a path ending at your email. Forgot password. Magic link. One-time code. "Confirm it's you."

That makes your inbox the root of trust for everything else you own.

And an inbox is a shared-secret account: reachable from anywhere, recoverable by a support process, protected by a password and maybe an SMS code a SIM swap can redirect.
Email was designed for trusted networks. It was never meant to be custodian of every other account you hold — it became that by accident, because it was the one identifier everybody already had.

Which means your security isn't the strength of your strongest login.

It's the strength of your weakest RECOVERY path.

For most people that's a mail account already compromised somewhere.

The alternative is older than the problem: stop sharing secrets.

You keep a private key. The service keeps only the matching public key. You prove identity by signing a challenge.

The service never holds anything an attacker can use.
That's what passkeys do, and it's no longer niche — FIDO reporting puts the installed base in the billions, with Google describing 800M+ accounts actively using them.

The important bit: a passkey signature is cryptographically BOUND to the site that requested it. A convincing fake can't replay it.

That removes phishing as a mechanism, instead of asking users to be better at spotting fakes.

And structurally, that's exactly what a crypto wallet is.

A wallet is a key pair with a balance attached. Signing a transaction and signing a login challenge are the same operation on different objects.

The reason to notice isn't tribal. It's that the industry arrived at the same answer twice, independently, for the same reason:

the only secret that can't be stolen from a server is one the server never had.
So why do legacy systems keep losing this fight? Not because they're old. Because they're CUSTODIAL by design — and custody creates an override.

If a provider can restore your access when you lose it, then a procedure exists that transfers control of your account to whoever completes it convincingly.

A support agent. A reset flow. A recovery channel.

That override is the feature people rely on most and the single most reliable thing to attack.

You can't fully patch it, because removing it means telling a locked-out customer that nothing can be done.

Every large consumer platform resolves that tension in favour of recoverability.

Which is why social engineering keeps working against companies with genuinely excellent engineering.

A blockchain account is structurally different, not incrementally better.

The account IS the key pair. No administrator, so no override to socially engineer. No reset flow to subvert. No credential database to breach — because there's no database.

It's also unforgiving, and the honest version says so in the same breath: no override means when a key is gone, it's gone.

The real task isn't picking between the two models. It's recovery that doesn't reintroduce a skeleton key.

Now the claim doing the most work in crypto security marketing — and deserving the most scepticism.

Ethereum is NOT quantum-resistant today.
Account signatures use elliptic-curve crypto a large enough quantum computer would break. Google Quantum AI research (Mar 2026) estimated ~1,200 logical qubits to break 256-bit ECC.

The Ethereum Foundation's post-quantum roadmap is serious and public: signature abstraction at the account level, hash-based signatures replacing validator BLS, proof systems for the much larger signatures.

It targets core PQ infrastructure around 2029.

Real work. Credible people. Right direction.

And close to nothing to do with the breaches in the first half of this thread.

Post-quantum crypto protects against a future adversary who can break today's maths.

It does nothing about a phishing page, an unpatched server, a stolen session cookie, or a support agent who believed a good story.

Anyone selling quantum resistance as the answer to the CURRENT security crisis is answering a different question on a different clock.

(The one real overlap: "harvest now, decrypt later" — an argument about long-lived secrets, not logins.)

And wallets don't fix everything. Moving to keys deletes one category of attack and creates two.

You can lose the key permanently. And attackers followed.

The dominant attack on wallet users isn't cracking keys. It's persuading people to SIGN something.

The cryptography works perfectly and signs exactly what it was asked to.
Phishing didn't disappear when the industry moved to keys. It moved from "give me your password" to "approve this" — harder to spot, because what you're approving is often unreadable.

Where we sit, including the uncomfortable part.

Swop is fully self-custodial — keys are generated and held on your device; Swop never holds them. Wallets run on Privy today. You can export your private key.

And the honest bit: Swop supports sign-in passkeys, but adding one does NOT switch email off.

It adds a second door rather than closing the first. By itself that's a convenience upgrade, not a security boundary.

That's not a Swop quirk — it's how most passkey rollouts quietly deliver less than they appear to.

The setting that actually changes your exposure is Transaction Security in Wallet Settings. It's separate, and it's off unless you turn it on.

With it on, someone who gets into your account still can't move funds without your passkey.

If you read one line of this thread as an instruction, make it that one.

For completeness: Swop has not commissioned a third-party security audit to date.

What we owe people is what the industry owes them: recovery that doesn't reintroduce a skeleton key.

A passkey that makes email INSUFFICIENT, not just optional. Step-up checks on actions that move value. A self-custody backstop for anyone who wants out.

The last of those exists today. The first two are the work.

Not security advice. The question worth carrying: not "is the encryption strong" — it is — but "who can get my access without my key?"
